title: Optional for absent values
idea: `Optional<T>` is a return type that says a value may be missing, so the caller must choose what happens then instead of meeting `null` later.
points: Return `Optional` from lookups like `findById`; the signature now documents absence.
`map` and `filter` run only on a present value; an empty one passes through.
End the chain with `orElse`, `orElseGet` or `orElseThrow` to pick the fallback.
Use it for return values only, not for fields, parameters or collections.

hero.title: One lookup through an Optional chain

steps.caption: `findById` finds customer c3 and wraps it. The `Optional` is present.
`map` runs because a value is present. The box now holds the email string.
`filter` tests for an @ sign. The test fails, so the result is an empty `Optional`.
`map` on an empty `Optional` does nothing. The lambda never runs, so it cannot crash.
`orElse` unwraps: a present value comes out as is, an empty one becomes the fallback.
`orElseThrow` is the strict ending: empty becomes a clear exception here, not a null crash later.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: A lookup that returns `null` without saying so, and a caller that trusts it.

walk.text: The map is immutable and safe, but `get` still returns `null` for a missing key.
`findEmail` passes that `null` on. Nothing in its return type warns the caller.
`emailDomain` calls `indexOf` on the result. For an unknown id that dereferences `null`.
The crash happens in `emailDomain`, far from the lookup that caused it. Real code rarely catches it.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: `findById` returns `Optional`, and each caller chooses a fallback or a clear failure.

walk.text: `ofNullable` wraps a lookup that may be null; `of` throws on null. Absence is now in the type.
The record rejects null fields, so values inside an `Optional` are always complete.
`map` extracts, `filter` rejects bad emails, `map` cuts the domain. Empty skips every step.
`orElse` with a constant suits display code that must always show something.
`orElseThrow` with a supplier suits callers that need a value. The message names the id.
Three ids cover the three paths: present, missing, and present but invalid.

pitfalls: Calling `get()` without a check just moves the crash; use `orElseThrow` to state intent.
`orElse(load())` always runs `load`, even when present; use `orElseGet` for costly fallbacks.
Returning `null` from a method typed `Optional` defeats it; return `Optional.empty()`.

quiz.why: `orElse` takes a value, so `guest()` runs before the call. `orElseGet` takes a supplier and calls it only when empty.

takeaway: Return `Optional` for maybe-missing results; end every chain with a fallback.
